utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and outside. Before the next witness is being brought in, the Chamber would like to raise a matter. If we understood the motion correctly, you are dealing with two maps, marked maps, one list of exhibits and one intercept transcript. Do you intend to use these documents with the witness of today, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to you, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. President. I do intend to use two of the exhibits with Ms. Frease. Those are the maps that are referred to in the -- in the motion. With respect to the list, that relates -- well, there's two maps and intercept that I plan to use with Ms. Frease. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll have to check with Ms. Stewart if you just bear with me for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart informs me that they were disclosed together with the filing or in the filing themselves, and I've explained the purpose of the maps also, I think, contemporaneously with the filing in an e-mail to Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will not deal with the list of documents because they -- the Prosecution doesn't intend to use them with this witness, Ms. Frease, but, Mr. Tolimir, are you in a position to give us your opinion about the two maps and the one intercept? utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome to the Tribunal. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and please sit down. I think you know the procedure in this Tribunal, and Mr. Vanderpuye has, I suppose, some questions for you. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you, again. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I suppose we'll get right to it, and let me ask you, do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Popovic et al. on 19, 25 -- 19 and 25 January, 26th and 27th February, and 1st and 2nd and 5th and 6th of March, 2007?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was the testimony that you gave at the time truthful?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to read and review your testimony prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it fairly and accurately reflect what you would say were you to be examined and asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I would move to admit the witness's previous testimony and the attendant exhibits related to it -- or associated exhibits, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

It's P787, 88, 89, 90 through -- through 800; 801 through 822; 823 through 834; 835 through 840A, B, and C; 841A and B; 842; 843A and B and C; 844; 845A and B; 846; 847A, B, and C; 848; 849; 850A and B; 851A and B; 852; 853 through 855; 836A -- I'm sorry, 856 -- all right. It is 836A and then 856, 857, 858, 841 -- I'm sorry, that's 841C, 843D, 845C, 859 through 863.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- the internal memorandum of the Registry of yesterday. Then we have it clear on the record. But not every document has a translation yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that the following documents don't have a translation. They could only be marked for identification pending translation, these are: P766A and B, 772 and 773, 781. This is, I was told, an audio but no transcript. P804, P810, P812, P815, P826A and B, P827. The Prosecution has indicated that only the first page will be translated. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's correct. I think that's correct, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you are tendering all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the exhibits and the list of the internal memorandum of yesterday in the parts I, II and III because they were used with the witness and received in the other trial, Popovic, and we will see how to deal with the exhibits which were not admitted yet under IV of the list. We will see how to deal with that during this examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a surprisingly brief summary for this witness, but I do also intend to ask her a substantial number of questions following it. From April 1995 to July 2000, the witness worked as an analyst in the Office of the Prosecutor. During this period, she was assigned to the Srebrenica investigation. The witness testified about the circumstances under which the OTP obtained the collection of ABiH radio intercept material. In particular, she testified about notebooks containing handwritten transcriptions of intercepted radio communications, electronic data containing typewritten versions of these intercepts, hard copies of this typewritten material, as well as audiotapes of intercepts. The witness also testified as to the manner in which the OTP investigated the reliability and authenticity of these intercept-related materials. The witness testified that after some initial efforts, the OTP first began to acquire ABiH radio intercept -- intercept material in 1998. The OTP received this material in several batches over a period of years, eventually resulting in a voluminous collection of intercept-related material. The witness was directly involved in the acquisition of this material and became a key figure in its processing within the OTP. Together with members of various sections within the OTP, the witness worked closely with this intercept material for approximately two years. She formed and supervised a team of interpreters and language assistants to process the material and helped to develop a system whereby the materials could be reliably tracked and searched. The witness was involved in creating a database of intercept materials which facilitated the ability to analyse and cross-reference the information contained in various forms of the intercepted communications, for example, audio, handwritten, and typewritten versions. Military analysts were consulted and involved in this process and assisted in analysing information from the intercept material and in linking its contents to the facts uncovered during the course of the OTP's investigation into the events surrounding Srebrenica. The witness testified that from the very beginning the OTP began to receive intercept-related materials, one of the OTP's main objectives was to evaluate its reliability, its accuracy and its authenticity. This was a continual process whereby the intercept team examined hard copy typewritten versions of the intercepts, original notebooks containing transcriptions of intercepted communications, audio recordings of intercepted communications, where available, as well as electronic versions of the typewritten material provided to the OTP on computer disks. The electronic versions of the typewritten intercepts were carefully evaluated against hard copy versions of the same intercepts which had earlier been provided to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please slow down for the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While the hard copy versions suffered from problems commonly associated with poor photocopying, such as poor legibility at the top and bottom of pages, the material revealed no substantive differences. The witness also compared the electronic and hard copy versions of the typewritten intercepts to the handwritten transcriptions contained in the original notebooks and found that they substantially conformed. Several ABiH intercept operators were identified by the OTP during the course of investigating the reliability of the intercept material. These operators were interviewed by the OTP and provided information concerning the interception process which further supported the reliability of the material. The manner in which the intercepted communications were transcribed into the notebooks by the intercept operators was also closely scrutinised. Markings in the notebooks such as words that had been crossed out or changes in the handwriting or ink used to make entries were investigated, discussed with the intercept operators, and explanations were sought. It was through this continual process of scrutinising the intercept material, as well as cross-referencing it over a number of years, that any initial skepticism as to the provenance or reliability of the intercept material was dispelled, and the OTP gained sufficient confidence in the authenticity and reliability of this material. The witness testified that despite inconsistencies that she came across during years of dealing with the intercept materials, she never came across any intercept that caused her to question the authenticity or reliability of the intercept collection as a whole. This concludes my summary, Mr. President. And as I -- as I mentioned, I do have a number of questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: By way of background, Ms. Frease, can you tell us what work you do now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: From the last time I was here, I continued to work for the Office of the Prosecutor as a special advisor through about the end of the year 2007. I then returned to the United States and did some consultancy work. In the last 18 months I've been working for a consultancy firm in Southern Sudan as a manager, and the consultancy firm provides support to the US agency for international development.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could remind us, how long did you work for the OTP over the -- during the time that you were there, from the first -- when you first arrived until you left? How many years was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I started in April of 1995 and left in July of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And during that period, how long did you work with the OTP team that was investigating the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was among the first people who went out to begin the investigation on Srebrenica one week after the events had occurred. I then worked on other projects within the OTP but was substantially involved in the Srebrenica investigation for the entire period that I was with the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the course of your involvement with the investigation of the Srebrenica events, in what capacity did you work?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was a research officer and an analyst and participated in a lot of the field investigations and analytical work here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the analytical work that you did, could you just give us a sense, very briefly a sense of what kind of things you did.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I did a lot of -- looked a lot at documents, evaluated documents, and then the intercept project, of course, required a lot of deep and detailed analytical work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was it that you first became involved in these intercept-related matters?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In the spring of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about how that came about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In the summer, in July of 1995, we had learned or heard that there were, in fact, intercepted conversations, but we weren't able to obtain them at that time. Finally, by about the end of 1997, the situation had changed somewhat on the ground, and in the spring of 1998 we were -- the OTP was given access to the preliminary -- some of the preliminary material from -- that had been intercepted during that period of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And once you -- well, were you involved, actually, in -- in obtaining this initial materials that -- these first intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. That was obtained by the team leader, Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the OTP's ability to get the intercept material following its identification, could you describe the level of co-operation the OTP received from the Bosnian authorities in terms of -- in terms of getting access to this material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Could you clarify your question, which periods you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Initial. The initial periods after 1995 when -- when it was learned that there were potentially intercepts to be gotten, were there efforts made by the OTP to get them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the efforts made by the OTP, were the Bosnian authorities forthcoming in providing access to the material or the materials themselves?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you -- do you know why that might be or why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can speculate as to why that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd rather not -- you not speculate.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you know then -- then you know or not. But in terms of your evaluation ultimately of the reliability and authenticity of the materials, did you consider the circumstances under which they were obtained, whether or not they were given freely or they were given -- or the Bosnian authorities were reluctant to give it to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how so? How did you consider it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer this question, I would like to remind both speakers as you are using the same language, it's very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything. Please pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. When I first began to review the material, I reviewed it with, I would say, a healthy degree of skepticism, and there were always questions in my mind and in the minds of other people that worked on this material about whether or not the material was, in fact, genuine, and whether we could rely upon it for its accuracy. So I would say that the entire time that I worked on the material and that the team worked on the material that we always scrutinised it and worked hard to make sure that we felt it was both genuine and reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Ms. Frease. I'd like to show you a document. Just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: P791, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to see that on the screen, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a receipt that was written, produced by the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, dated the 3rd of March, 1998, written in the name of -- to Jean-Rene Ruez, the investigation team leader, for materials handed over -- for radio intercepted material reports handed over on the 3rd of March relating to VRS intercepted communication. That's Bosnian Serb army communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the transcript we seem to have the witness saying written by the commander. In any case, this document was not signed by the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps we should be more precise and say that it was signed by Captain -- I can't really make out the name. Adnan. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Vanderpuye will try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think the document speaks for itself. It indicates a person by the name of Captain Adnan. Then it also has a stamp which indicates 2nd Corps Deputy Commander Brigadier Sulejman Budakovic, and there's also a signature that indicates the initials JR Ruez. These are all at the bottom of the document, and I think -- yeah, we do have the original in -- we have the original in e-court for everyone to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know what -- I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was just going to clarify that when I started, I mentioned the command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And this Mr. Adnan, I think this is only the first name and there is a family name which is partly unlegible, something like Cohodarovic or something like that, just for the record. Please carry on Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now with respect to the assembled radio reports, do you know what that refers to particularly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. I worked on these a lot. It was a compilation of about 550 pages of photocopied, typed out, compiled reports that were handed over to us in a binder, over to the OTP in a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall what period of time these particular intercepts covered?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: From the 9th of July until the 30th or 31st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's P792 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's loading, let me just ask, with respect to this material, was that material specifically requested by the Office of the Prosecutor or was it -- or was it selected and turned over by the Bosnian Army on their own?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We had requested the intercepted material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know whether or not this material relates to the Srebrenica events solely or whether it comprises other information that was gained through the army's radio interception unit?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We were specifically interested in the Srebrenica events, but my memory is that there were also some conversations in that binder that didn't necessarily relate to those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's now in e-court?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's the cover page for those 550 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the 550 pages of hard copied intercept material, were there any differences between that material and the printouts from the electronic data that the OTP received subsequently?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, there were differences. A couple of the differences were that the headers on the various -- we learned later that the headers on the various reports were missing, and also when we first started looking at this material, we noticed that there were -- some of the reports were written in typical sentence structure, typed in typical sentence structure with a capital letter at the beginning of a sentence and then small case letters throughout, where other reports, other messages, were typed in all caps and were usually, in fact almost always, they started with a particular type of comment, like on the -- I can't -- I can't quite remember it right now, but like, On this particular day at this particular time, on these frequencies we intercepted communication between this person and this person or X and Y, and then it would continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And at the time that you received this material or shortly thereafter, did you rely on this material? Did you consider it reliable in terms of further investigations?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We were using it at the time as an investigative tool, and we worked with it for a number of months in analysing it first before we moved on to analysing the notebooks. I would say that when we first started we were still unsure about its reliability.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following your receipt of this set of intercepts, did you receive -- well, you did receive, I should say, other notebook -- notebooks or handwritten transcriptions of the intercepts. Do you know approximately when that was when you received them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We received them in April of 1998, though they had been identified in March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that during the course of a mission in order to obtain the materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show you P285 in e-court, please. And while that's loading let me ask you, do you recall approximately how many notebooks you received initially?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: One hundred and thirty-four plus one, which I guess makes it 135, but I say plus one because the last one was something like a log that wasn't used to transcribe conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're not broadcasting this, are we? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the document that's on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: A list of the notebooks, an inventory of the notebooks that we identified as being significant to the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just want to draw your attention to the top left corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can blow that up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You can see a date there that's indicated of 11 March 1998. Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the date that you received this material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you can see the translation on the right-hand side which says: "Breakdown of 2nd Corps documents (office archive and intercepts) submitted to the ICTY representatives." But is it the case that it wasn't submitted on that day?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall what day these documents were actually turned over to the Office of the Prosecutor or when?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In April of 1998. We were hoping at the time that they would be turned over in March, but we received word on the 12th of March that we needed official approval from the Ministry of Defence to have them turned over, so they were turned over on the following mission in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I just want to show you the next document which is P284, and I want to see if you can confirm to us that this list that's on the screen now, 285, is what's referred to in this next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We're not broadcasting this one either, I take it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you can see on the document, the original on the -- on the left, you can see your name right in the middle of it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The document purports that a total of 135 documents were registered and listed and duly packed into a cardboard box. This is in the second paragraph, just so the Court is familiar with where I'm reading from. They were packed into a cardboard box containing the signatures of the representatives of The Hague Tribunal, Peter Nicholson and an unnamed representative of the command of the 2nd Corps. And it says a list of the individual documents is appended to this record, 1 through 135. Does this refer to the list that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does this document accurately reflect the date that the documents were, in fact, handed over to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's indicated here as 20 April 1998. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in addition to this material did you receive any other material on or around this -- on this date or around this period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. We -- we received some tapes, some reel-to-reel tapes. On the -- I received 13 on the 25th of April, and it was during this time that there was -- we had a mission to Tuzla with a -- an expert in reel-to-reel communication analysis. He received 19 tapes in Tuzla on the 25th of April, and then I drove down to Sarajevo and picked up 13 more tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the tapes that you picked up, the 13 tapes, were those returned to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Did I deliver them to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was that documented?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to see the documentation concerning that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And does it confirm what you've recounted to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now I'd like to show you P289.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: P289, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: While that's loading, let me ask you, with respect to the 13 tapes that you picked up, do you know whether or not those tapes contained anything of significance to the Srebrenica investigation, or what's your recollection about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I see we have 289 in -- in e-court now. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this document indicates that it's a record of transfer of archival material gathered through ER, I assume it's electronic reconnaissance, regarding the events in Srebrenica in 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it purports -- well, it says, I should say, that a total of 19 tapes was found and listed, with signs made by Jack Hunter, with additional signs on slips of paper placed in each box with the tapes. That's in the second paragraph. And it says: "A list of the separate tapes is enclosed with this record and handwritten by Jack Hunter from number Q1 through Q19." You recognise this, I take it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is this the event that you've just testified about concerning his receipt of 19 tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And also in the fourth paragraph it indicates that the tapes were handed over to Jack L. Hunter Jr., US army, and it provides a social security number. Do you know whether Mr. Hunter was a member of the US army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. My information was that he -- well, he worked for ATF, which is Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms organisation in the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is Mr. Hunter the expert in radio communications or radio tape devices that you were talking about -- I'm sorry, tape devices that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he take custody of those tapes for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know what, if anything, he did with those tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: He took them to his lab in Washington, DC, and analysed them, made copies, provided copies back to us along with the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, following the receipt of these tapes in 1998, you received some additional notebooks in 1999. Is that -- is that right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you remember approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In May of 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P286. While that's loading, let me ask you, do you know approximately what intercept-related materials you received then? How many notebooks, or if there were other materials, what those were?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I received additional notebooks, 55 additional notebooks, that I think turned out to be not so significant because they recorded different tactical level communications and coded communication. Nonetheless, we did receive those and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we have the document on the screen now, and I hope we're not broadcasting it. Great. You can see your signature on the bottom right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And this document says that you were handed over -- well, you were handed over this material which is 55 A-5 format notebooks, A-4 format notebooks. Well, there's one. And a -- two 1.4 megabyte diskettes together with a diary.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the information that was on the diskettes, do you recall what that information was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I recall that we weren't able to open the diskettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You mean electronically or a physical package?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right. Electronically we weren't able to get into them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you recall if 10th May was the day you actually received this material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's my recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another document, which is P287, and we'll need to go -- well, first we'll stay on the first page so we can make the record clear. Do you recognise this document, first of all?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it indicates it's a record of hand-over of archived material to the investigative team at The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could go to the second page in the B/C/S and it will be the third page in English, first I will just note that on this first page it says the archive material was handed over to Stefanie Frease. And it indicates that it was given by Sevko Tihic, head of G2 department, on 10 May 1999. And I want to draw your attention in particular to lines 46 through 49 of this document. And in -- do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And line 46 refers to 55 pieces, A-5 notebooks. Line 47 refers to 4 A-4 notebooks, and 48 refers to the two disks or to two disks, and 49 refers to this shift agenda.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does this document relate to or is this document referring to the same material that was provided to you in the document we saw previously, which was P286?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we please see the first page again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'd like to compare the dates. We see there the entry Tuzla, 14th of May, 1999, but it relates to hand-over of the 10th of May, 1999; is that correct? Just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, but I -- maybe the witness should answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as long as -- as long as the question is asked, can you -- do you know why there was a difference of four days between the two of these documents?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know or can you recall whether there were additional transfers of tapes to the OTP following your receipt of this -- this material in 1999? Do you know if there were additional transfers that occurred in 2000?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us a little bit about that, what you can remember?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Are you referring to the -- to additional military handovers or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, military handovers.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you a document. If you can just hang on one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. It's P38. If I could have that in e-court, please. Oh, I'm sorry, 838, P838.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. What we have here is a document that concerns a search of the -- well, ARBiH archives located at Ramiz Salcin barracks, Otoka, Sarajevo. Do you have any familiarity with this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a record of a search that took place by a different OTP team --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: -- during which tapes were seized. It was after the time that I left the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how did you come to know about this particular document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I was shown it by members of the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And was that in preparation for your testimony in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to page -- I think it's page 3, and what this reflects --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document P858 did not have a translation into the language I understand, into Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It was P838.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: There are quite a lot of documents without translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- that's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the case of the accused, it could be helpful to indicate a little bit further what is the content of the document so that Mr. Tolimir can understand that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Well, what we can do is -- well, let's go back to the first page and I can read into the record a little bit what this document says so that we can familiarise Mr. Tolimir with it. This is a document that's entitled "Inventory and receipt of property obtained during the execution of a consensual search conducted by the ICTY." And it reads in the first paragraph: "I hereby certify that between 1830 and 0400 hours on the 16th and 17th day of October, 2000, at the archive of the former ARBiH archives located at Ramiz Salcin barracks, Otoka, Sarajevo, a consensual search was conducted by the following staff of the ICTY," and the names are indicated. In the -- following the names it indicates -- it reads: "With the consent and co-operation of the person charged with assisting the ICTY at the premises, namely, Major Ramezic Suad and Major Adem Omerkic, and the attached inventory consisting of 4 pages listing 20 items is a true and accurate record of the items handed over during the search." Now, if we can go to page 3, and it's really for a very limited purpose of this document, you can see that there's a date, 16 October 2000, and next to it is written that 100 centimetres by 75 centimetres by 50 centimetres box containing numerous audiotape and other -- and a number of audio magnetic reels. And then it lists a number of cassettes tapes that were marked with numbers, and in this case you can see that there are numbers 1 going all the way to 192. And then if we go to the following page, you will see there's another box, 17 October, same size, hundred centimetres by 75 by 50, and it's containing 98 audio magnetic reels, and these are numbered 1 in sequence, I think, all the way up to 114. Now, with respect to these reel tapes, are you aware of any significant -- or tapes that were significant to the Srebrenica investigation that were recovered from this batch of material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recall as significant to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe that it was tape 49 that corroborated a conversation that was on a tape that was handed over to Jack Hunter on the 25th of April, 1998, tape number Q2, and that we found the same conversation recorded from two different sites. So they were slightly different in terms of their content, but they were clearly the same conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of the document we have a handwritten note, the 17th of October, 2000. Could that please be explained, and perhaps there is an explanation as to who inserted that note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think what Mr. Tolimir's referring to is a signature, and it's the signature of Daniel Perry. D Perry is what that says and it's date next to it, 17 October 2000. I think that's what you're referring. Please correct me if I am wrong. It's on two pages. I should say, I'm sorry, it's on each page of the inventory sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can ask the witness about this signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, are you familiar with the signature of Mr. Perry?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you identify whether it is a signature on the bottom of the sheet or something else?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It looks like a signature. It also looks like there could be another signature on the right side. Probably the Bosnian counterpart would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just for the record, tape 49 that the witness is referring to is P509. It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you made a reference just now to tape --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, just a moment, please. Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Just a clarification. At page 27, lines 23 to 24, you have stated that: "So they were slightly different in terms of their content, but they were clearly the same conversation." Can you just elaborate on that, how there was a difference in content but clearly the same conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This was something that -- that puzzled us a lot at the beginning, but what we learned was that when conversations were recorded at the two different sites, one site could hear sometimes some of the participants better than others, than the one at the other site. So they mutually -- they helped -- they helped to fill out the conversation usually, because on one side you would have some -- I guess as I've just said, you could hear some of the people because of the location of the antenna and the way that they could pick up the frequency and where the particular conversation was taking place, you may have one area that could pick up the conversation better and maybe both sides of the conversation, where maybe in this other location, you would have it also recorded, the intercept operator could tell it was an important conversation but perhaps could only hear one side of the conversation. So in this example, we had a situation where we had tapes -- we had recorded conversations that had come from different two sites that had slightly different content because of the fact that they were recorded in two different locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I was asking you about your reference to Q1 and Q2, and with respect to the tapes that Mr. Hunter received, Q1 through 19, do those tapes also contain significant information, other than the reference that you've given now concerning the Srebrenica investigation, the Srebrenica events?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me move forward. I'd like to show you P288. All right. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what -- what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a receipt signed by Jean-Rene Ruez, again the team leader for the Srebrenica investigation, from 2 Corps in Tuzla in which he received additional -- yeah, additional documentation and information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And with respect to the specific reference here to station diaries with data collected by the electronic reconnaissance EIV, platoon I think that might mean, or company, it says 42 pieces. Do you know what that means, what they're talking about or what's referred to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Those are 42 additional notebooks is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And there's a reference here to 1.44 megabyte diskettes. It indicates seven of them. Do you know what that relates to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Those are the electronic versions, the typed versions of the conversations that were sent from the locations to 2 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these are the electronic versions that we've been referring to that were compared against the hard copy, are they one and the same?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct, except that these were more complete because they had the headers and the footers. So the -- when we first talked about the 550 pages that we received, and I mentioned that the headers were missing and sometimes lines were missing at the bottom of conversations towards the bottom of the page, these reflected the complete conversations as they were reflected also in the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we could just go over to Annex 2 of this document. That should be page 3 in the English, and I think it should be the same in B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Here you see it indicates a list of station diaries from 1995. It indicates the paper size is A5. These are the notebooks to which you've referred?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the notebooks that you received initially and up until this point, did they contain these similar entries, similar markings such as the registration information? We see here, "SP: 08/2-01-496," for example, in the first line. It indicates a date -- well, sorry, in the second line it indicates a date of 4 July 1995, and then a period from 12 July to 21 July 1995. Was that typical of the material that you received prior to this time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you yourself, by the way, document the material that you received in terms of entering this information as well?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to the next annex, that's Annex number 3. It should be the next page in both documents. Sorry, I have to go one more in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what we have here, it says review of 1.44 megabyte diskettes with RI reports. And can you confirm that the period covered by the electronic data that was received here from January, it appears, through December 1995, is -- is accurate?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I didn't look at every diskette.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sure, but my question, and I'm sorry it was a bit unartful, but does your recollection correspond with this, that the material that was received at this time concerned basically the calendar year for 1995 as opposed to 1994, 1996, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'd like to move ahead. Now, in terms of your recollection of the events concerning the chain of custody of these materials, were you able to confirm that in any other documents, in anything you looked at?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In some internal reports, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just bear with me one moment. I'd like to show you another document. I'd like to show you P856, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand this document doesn't have a translation as well, so I will just read the caption off so that Mr. Tolimir can understand what it is. The caption reads -- oh, there it is. There is a translation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you had an opportunity to review it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Does it comport with your recollection of the events concerning the transfer or receipt of intercept-related material as you've testified to today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And what I'd like to ask you is that following this -- actually, not following this but separately from this, do you have a specific recollection of the circumstances under which the OTP received intercept materials from the MUP security forces of the -- of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us a little bit about that, please.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We received material from the SDB in Tuzla in May of 1999, and that came in the form of a lot of typed reports, a lot of typed conversations, and also some diskettes, some electronic versions.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.text: And if we can go to the next page of this document.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: On the following page -- we can go to the following page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to the next page --

utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness is testifying about the material that was not in the possession of the Tribunal until the 28th of August, 2001, so it's a little bit strange how you can testify about material that was not in the possession of the OTP when -- once the witness was no longer employed there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that's a fair point, but I think it's also clarified for Mr. Tolimir by the fact that the witness reviewed and used these materials in preparation for her testimony in the Popovic case, which as you know occurred in 2007, and that's the reason why it's relevant. It's a relevant question to put to the witness about her familiarity with the chain of custody and the documents that establish the authenticity or the provenance of the materials with which she worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, the Chamber has to consider this way of evidence because, in fact, you could put every document to every witness in proofing or in testimony and then ask later about the authenticity.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is one additional ground, Mr. President, and that is the document that I referred to before this one, which is P828, was turned over to the Tribunal, as you may recall, on the 27th of July, 1999. It lists in there, in that document, the report numbers for the materials which were received then, which correspond to the report numbers which are indicated in the document that I've just put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We'll consider that during the break, but before we break, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just need some clarifications for me to better understand the unfolding testimony. What is SDB?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's a term that is used for -- okay. In the -- in the former Yugoslavia, during the war there were various types of police, sort of the traffic police, there was the secret police, and then there were different regional units and sub-units. And so the CSB, for example, would have been -- I can't remember now exactly how many there were, but, say, something like seven in Bosnia-Herzegovina that would have comprised regional areas. The SDB was for a smaller area, and that was for the police but considered more the secret police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Then you also refer -- I don't know, not necessarily you, maybe Mr. Vanderpuye could shed some light for me. What are RI reports?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said "RI reports." Those are radio intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then one last question for the witness. In your earlier testimony you said that there was some resistance by the BiH authorities to hand over documents or intercepts initially; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Why do you think there was this resistance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, in 1995, the war was still going on and radio intercepted communication is extremely sensitive. It's sort of like considered like the crown jewels of any kind of intelligence gathering operation. They use the material in realtime to forward to their command posts, either to protect their own people or to forward information that they considered relevant. At the time we hadn't established a relationship with them, and because the war was still going on, I think that there was understandable hesitation and resistance to handing over this very sensitive material to a group of people that they didn't know and didn't necessarily know if they could trust. If that material had been leaked, it could have compromised very sensitive information from their side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think we must have our first break now, and you should consider the concern of Mr. Tolimir, and we will do that as well, and we will resume five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, the Registry has to make a correction of a certain document number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. P826B has been provisionally admitted pending translation as public by mistake. It has to be marked as under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. We have to come back to the previous document and to discuss the concerns of Mr. Tolimir. utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President. I think I can explain it in two ways. The first way is more direct. It relates to the content of the document itself. Okay. I'll need -- I think I'll need both in e-court if we can do that. It was P828. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, and P827. Okay. With respect to the document that's now -- the documents that are now in e-court, the Court can see that the document on the left has the date 27 July 1999, and it refers to intercept reports that the witness testified about earlier, and you can see on the left, immediately to the left of each date a report number. utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE

utterances.text: And if you -- if you know the answer to that question, Ms. Frease, could you -- could you answer it, and if you don't, just say so.

utterances.text: Thanks. Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could help us with this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, does that clarify the situation? Are you satisfied with these explanations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I am not. utterances.text: But with respect to the document on the right, that's 827.
