utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that's the same heading as the previous document?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the source of the same -- the same source of the information that was provided --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- in this one? And if we go to the second page of this document. 827. Under number 1, next to number 1, you can see it says -- well, it seems to say disks for the month of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And as I've indicated before, if we go to the next page you can see disks for the month of July 1995. Do you see that on the -- it's not there yet. Okay. Do you see that there now, disks for July 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell me what your understanding is as concerns the report numbers that are indicated in 827 as they relate to the report numbers indicated in document 828? That's the one that we just looked at.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They are the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think it's important also to establish the nature of your familiarity with this material, and so I wanted to ask you a little bit about how it is that you came to know, and if you know, first, about these MUP or SDB intercept reports. Have you been involved in handling these reports or reviewing them?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if you could just tell the Trial Chamber how that came about and what is the nature of your familiarity with this material.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: When I -- when I started to look at the material in 1998, in April, and saw that some of the reports -- and now I'm referring back to the 550 pages, noticed in those 550 pages that there was some material that was in all caps with a particular heading. It wasn't clear for almost a year what the difference was, why some were written in that way, typed in that way, and some weren't. When we began to conduct interviews with the intercept operators and learned that there was this police unit that was also operating at the northern site and then we spoke with the police about this, that was when it became clear that the reports -- some of the reports originated from the military and some of the other reports originated from the police, but that they were sharing the information to their headquarters. So I worked with this information a lot, got to know it very well from the time that we received these documents from the police. We had also, of course, been working with them before, just not knowing what their provenance was, where they came from during the preceding year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to work with this material when you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor in 2006?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Could you describe for the Trial Chamber what the nature of your involvement was with respect to this material and the intercepts generally that were used by the Prosecution in that case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to -- to see the complete reports and to work with information that the Office of the Prosecutor had received since the time that I had left the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what work did you do exactly, if you could -- if you could be a little bit more specific so the Trial Chamber gets a sense of what the nature and extent of your familiarity with this material is.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was very similar to the work that I had done previously in trying to match everything up and making sure that in testing the -- the reliability of the information, in cross-referencing it, in making sure that if there were any differences in -- in the different versions, including -- this does get a little confusing. I'll try to break it down. We wanted to ensure that we had the most complete records possible of the conversations. Sometimes we were working off of old translations that had come from our original work with the material that we received in 1998, where there were sentences missing at the bottom of some of these reports. So this material, the material that we received from the MUP in this case, but also the military later, was more complete because the reports had their own headers on them. They had the complete text. And so the work that I did in 2006 [Realtime transcript read in error "1996"] and early 2007 was to make sure that everything was coming together in the most complete form. At that time, of course, I was still looking for any inconsistencies. I was asking people on the team who had continued to work with the material during that time whether they had seen anything in the interim that caused them any concern or alarm, and I continued to reassure, I guess, myself that the material was genuine and that it was reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, are you aware of whether or not the OTP received, other than the tapes that are indicated here, or I should say, the recordings that were indicated in P827 -- I'm sorry, it was P828. Other than those recordings, are you aware of whether or not the OTP received other recordings of intercepted communications from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether or not any such recordings were received by the OTP during the time that you were working for the OTP in 2006?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Let me take you to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you move to the next area, Judge Nyambe has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I just need a clarification from the witness. At page 52 of the transcript, lines 9 to 14, you have stated that: "So the work I did in 1996 and through early 2007 was to make sure that everything was coming together in the most complete form." Can you just elaborate exactly what you did. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and I see a typo in the transcript. It should say 2006 and not 1996 and early 2007. This material is quite complex because of the way we received it. We received it in bits and pieces, and we needed to piece it all together as we got to, cross-reference it many times given that there were several units working at two different sites and that there was handwritten material and there was typewritten material and then there was -- there were fairly poor photocopies of material. So in working with it, we didn't get everything at one time, and then of course, the audio material as well. So having worked on it for a couple of years, to me I can look it at the various parts of it and understand it, but I think it's very difficult to understand if you haven't spent days and days and days and days and hours and hours going through it in incredible detail. So in 2000 -- late 2006 and 2007 when I came in, we had received additional information, and my work was to try to make the cross-referencing aspects of this as straightforward as possible, to present in as clear a manner as possible. So some of that involved making sure that we had the most complete translations of a particular conversation, and that would have involved going back to the original material that we received, the 550 pages in 1998, seeing that we were missing a few lines at the bottom of one page of a translation, looking at now the final reports that were later transmitted, provided to the OTP, looking at those, seeing that the conversations were identical up and to -- up to a certain point where then the information was missing. So I would identify that as a problem, because it was incomplete. And then submitting that piece or that intercept for translation along with the translation that had already been done. So that's the sort of thing that I'm talking about when I talk about trying to make the material as complete as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Following on your explanation, so what form did the end product take after you have your complete information? Did you add on the original documents, or did you produce a new document, or do you have pieces of this translation lying somewhere for comparison purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We didn't add anything. We simply took the -- took the complete record to ensure that the court had the complete record.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think I can -- I'll put some questions to the witness. I think maybe we can clear that up a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you say -- when you refer to incomplete material, are you referring to the -- are you referring to the hard copy material, or are you referring to the electronic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the difference between the hard copy and the electronic version, in your view, were those substantive differences?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you say they could be substantive differences, do you mean that the language or the words that were used are different or that there were words missing or changed or what?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The words were not different, they were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Trial Chamber why the words were missing, that is, words relating to the conversations themselves.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They would be missing because they wouldn't be photocopied. They'd be at the bottom of the page. We could sometimes see the faint type but we couldn't -- we couldn't read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when you talk about making sure that the court had the complete record, did that entail a comparison of that photocopied material with the printouts from the electronic material, the electronic intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the complete record that was provided to the court or prepared for the court, was that based upon the information that came from the electronic version of those intercepts or even the notebook version of those intercepts rather than the photocopies that were received in 1998? If you can recall.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can't say for certain. My hesitancy is that certainly the incomplete parts primarily came from the original document that we received, the 550 pages. So the subsequent information that we have -- had -- for example, on this document dated 1999, the 27th of July, 1999, I believe that those are complete records of -- so a complete form of the electronic version that was received in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you involved in any way in assembling or putting all of these intercepts together in 2006 for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how many intercepts did that involve, roughly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: A few hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did it involve intercepts that were received from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did it involve intercepts that were received from the 2nd Corps of that army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did it involve intercepts that were received from the 21st Division of that army?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did it involve intercepts that were received from the CSB?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: From the SDB, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were those -- how were those -- those intercepts assembled, if you can recall? Were they assembled chronologically? Were they assembled in another way?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, they were assembled chronologically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you involved in producing any kind of database or index or anything like that relating to those particular intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how so?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, the -- the index had largely been put together for the Popovic trial by the time I arrived. However, that index was based on work that I had done, that I had set up in 1998. In that index there were two different systems that we used to analyse this information and to cross-reference it in the analytical process. One was a simple Excel table, another was an access database that was developed, that helped us to be able to capture a lot of information that was coming through in the conversations, as well as information about which notebook a particular conversation was recorded in, what page number of the original 550 pages was that notebook conversation recorded on, who the intercept operators were who recorded the particular conversation. So I was very involved in that entire process.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were there efforts made to determine the report numbers or dates from the electronic version of the intercepts in order to arrive at the correct date of a given intercept, for the army intercepts, for example?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were those same efforts made in relation to identifying the source of the MUP intercepts? Was there a reference made to the report numbers or other identifying information?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. My recollection is that that came through fairly clearly in the -- in the reports that we got in July of 1999 from the police, from the SDB.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a document -- just bear with me for one moment. It's P763. First, I want to ask you if you recognise generally what this is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a list of code-names used by the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where do these code-names appear?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: They appear in the -- in a lot of the radio intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see at the bottom it says "Updated from ERN 0211-3816." You see that there?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, do you know -- are you familiar with the document that this particular exhibit updates?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you involved in producing such a document for the purposes of the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I don't have a specific recollection. It's certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do these names appear -- as far as you can recall, are these names code-names that appeared in the intercepts that you reviewed in preparation for that trial and also prior to testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, though I don't recall all of them appearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you another document, and that's -- I'm sorry, it's P758. And do you know generally what this document shows?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It shows the names that came up in the intercepted communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are you familiar with the names that came up in those conversations? Does this -- does this fairly represent or comport with your recollection of the names that you saw during your analysis of those materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, though again I would say that in the conversations I analysed, I don't recall all of these names having come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you involved in producing such a document for the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Oh, and let me ask, before I forget --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, objection. Does this document have anything to do with the persons who worked -- actually, who recorded or transferred the intercepted conversations onto tapes or diskettes? Actually, that is my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, could you clarify this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think Mr. Tolimir's objection is well taken. It's not intended to show who transcribed the intercepts. This has to do with the reliability and authenticity of the -- of the material that the witness is here to testify about. So I think I can ask a couple of questions that may clarify the issue somewhat. All right. We have the list of names on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's start with the first one. Do you have familiarity with who Lazar Acamovic was based upon your review of the intercepted conversations? Do you have a recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Specifically of him at this time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. How about Colonel Ljubisa Beara?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And how about Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Slobodan Cerovic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Zoran Carkic?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Major Radomir Furtula?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Herve Gobillard?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Milan Gvero?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Richard Holbrooke?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Not because of this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Bernard Janvier?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These are some of the names that appear, obviously, in this document here, and are you familiar with them during the course of your assessment analysis of the intercept materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And before I forget, did you have an opportunity to discuss this index of names of intercepted communications with anyone prior to your testimony today to learn what its relationship is to an exhibit that was submitted in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did you learn concerning this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That it was an expanded list of an exhibit that had been presented in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, that's P1084 in the Popovic case. And if we could just go back for a brief moment to a previous exhibit. It was 763. Okay. I have to correct something. This exhibit that we're looking now -- looking at now is what was P1084 in Popovic. The one that we looked at previously was P1085. So the index of names of intercepted communications was P1085 in Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is P1084 in Popovic. Did you have an opportunity to discuss this particular document with anybody prior to your testimony here today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you discuss or did you learn of what its relationship was to the exhibit that was presented in the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, that it was an expanded version of what was used in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it familiar to you? Are the names that are in here familiar to you based upon your review of the intercept evidence from the Popovic case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Many of them are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are they familiar to you based upon what is contained in the intercept materials?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you a couple of maps, and this should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just to clarify one matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You just indicated some numbers from the -- document numbers from the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But the -- all these documents have P numbers in our case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: These documents have P numbers in our case as well. That's correct. What I wanted to establish --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To link --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- apparently unsuccessfully. Yes, that's right. I wanted to establish what the relationship is between this document and the one that was -- that is admitted, actually, pursuant to the witness's Popovic testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I wanted to show you two maps, which is P784 first. Okay. Have you had an opportunity to see this map before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recognise the names that are indicated that are in blocks, Krivace IKM, Podzeplje IKM, 65th Protection Regiment base, and so on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And are those names familiar to you as a result of your analysis of the intercept materials that you've worked with?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Some of them are, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And which ones are, if you can say? Well, maybe I'll just ask you. Are you familiar with Krivace?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Podzeplje?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I'm familiar with it. I can't say with certainty whether that familiarity comes from the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with it. I'm very familiar with it. I can't say that it's specifically because of the intercept material --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: -- at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Borike IKM?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the Boksanica check-point?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm familiar with it, but I'm not sure that it's because of the intercept material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you another map, if I could, and that one is P785. Okay. Have you had an opportunity to see this map before testifying here today?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And this contains a lot of the same locations. You can see Godenje IKM, Boksanica check-point and Borike IKM over there on the right in the lower quadrant of the map. And then you can see Kravica IKM, Podzeplje IKM and the 65th Protection Regiment base that we talked about before, then you can see a town called Han Pijesak. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you know that to be where the VRS headquarters was located?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move to another area yet. And what I'd like to ask you about a little bit is the process by which you authenticated the intercept evidence just in a general way. Now, you've talked about it somewhat so I don't want you to -- I don't want to have you repeat yourself, but you engaged in what's -- you mentioned called the intercept project and from your prior testimony you prepared what's called -- what you called an authentication binder?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, just in very brief terms, what that project was about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you answer. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We should know when the witness saw these maps for the first time since she's testifying to their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. That's no problem. I should clarify. She's not testifying to the authenticity of the maps but she is testifying to her familiarity with the locations that are depicted in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: But if you could answer Mr. Tolimir's question as to when you saw these maps that would probably be helpful.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I saw them in the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And was that during the course of being proofed?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If you could tell us in really very basic terms what this authentic -- what process was involved in producing the authentication binder. Maybe you can tell us what it is generally and then tell us how you went about preparing it.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: In order to authenticate the intercepts, we wanted to be able to confirm their content and their validity by using other sources, and some of those sources involved notes that were taken by UN officials about conversations that they had with particular members as designated in particular conversations and where the time and date corresponded. So there were UN personnel, notes from UN personnel that we used. We used aerial imagery that corresponded to events that were discussed in the intercepted communication. We used sometimes small things like one person in a conversation would give the phone number of somebody else, a Serb living in Republika Srpska at the time. So we'd get the phone book, look up the person's name and find that that was the same phone number that had been transmitted in the intercepted communication. We looked at other sources as well but stayed away from anything that would have come from the Bosnian forces, from the Bosnian side, because we wanted to make sure that what we had was really independently verifiable.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in terms of the binder that you put together, was that -- how many intercepts did that involve?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: About a dozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is there a particular reason why a dozen of these intercepts were -- were verified or processed in this way rather than the entire collection of intercepts that were available to the Prosecution at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was just a very vivid selection. It would have been impossible to make that kind of an independent authentication of each conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in connection with what case did you prepare this authentication binder of material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The first time was for the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you prepare a second one?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And when was that, and for what case?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That was for the Popovic case, but a number of the same examples were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you first in terms of determining the reliability of a given intercept, if you could tell us aside from the -- the factors that you've indicated, what kinds of things did you look at specifically in respect of the intercept itself to determine or to consider in evaluating its reliability or accuracy?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: We looked at how the information fit into our knowledge of the overall case and whether there were any really significant or glaring differences in -- in what we knew and what was reflected there. Some of the other material that we used to authenticate the intercepts came from captured Bosnian Serb military documents, for example. But the reliability, there was -- I guess a lot of the reliability also came from our conversations with the intercept operators, because we had a lot of questions initially about, you know, why was it that there were certain conversations that we could tell were the same conversation but they weren't -- but we were getting different parts of them, and until we understood that there were two sites, four units working, and that they could have been recording the same conversation, we had some questions in our minds about -- I had questions in my mind about the reliability of this stuff. But in talking with the intercept operators and understanding the procedures that they used in recording them and that that was, in fact, an exercise in dictation, essentially, and not creative writing, and that they were very diligent in how they recorded the conversations, those factors contributed to the reliability that we could have internally on this body of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I -- what I'd like to do is to go over just a couple of illustrative examples of what you're talking about. I think it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber's understanding of the process.

Can you just focus on what features or procedures actually removed the doubts that you had initially on the reliability of this stuff, as you referred to it in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many different factors in -- that contributed. The intercept operators were instructed to sit down, to put on headphones and to write what they heard. When they came across a conversation that they thought was important, they would begin to record it. If they thought that it was important, they would begin to transcribe it right away. We heard -- when we started to interview the operators, they went through and explained similar procedures and that when they weren't sure of the people who were talking, that they were instructed to put question marks. If they heard clearly who the people who were talking were, then they would indicate those names at the top of the conversation and indicate the time. On the dates they were less consistent in the notebooks. Furthermore, all of the operators followed the same procedure, and later when we began to listen to the audiotapes, we could also hear that they were recording -- that they were transcribing the words that they heard recorded. So it was -- these were people who were selected to be in this unit in part because of their level of education and their ability to follow the procedures that had been laid out for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In other words, you did the same as the intercept operators did. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Also, later -- yes, we did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it has a number on it, 2140?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And next to that, in box number 6 it has a date?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. The 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go a little bit down this page to box number 14 and 15. That will be a little bit to the right too. You can see where it says name and address of the recipient.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that indicates "KDK."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right. The command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it says beneath that in box 15, "Addressee station." You see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what is --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It says "For Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go a little bit down the page, beneath box 25 and 26, it will be to your left, it specifies what's being ordered?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what does it say?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It says diesel fuel D2, and further down it says 500 litres of D2 fuel. And then it says 140 litres were returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, is this the original document? Are we talking about its authenticity, or is this a document created in English, because the Drina Corps didn't have any forms in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was going to ask the same question as you, Mr. Tolimir. I wanted to see -- when this document is finished to have the B/C/S original and so we can identify if it's the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately because the pages are in sequence they're not displaced side by side. Otherwise, I think we could have a translation of it. But as I've indicated, we do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's too small to have both versions on the screen at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Right. So we'll just go to the next page and I think we can clarify this very quickly. First, let's focus on the top right-hand corner like we did before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you can see there it says "Broj"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Top left-hand corner, "number."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it indicates the same number as before, 2140?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And next to that you can see "Datum"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That means "date," I take it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And it says 16.07.95?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go down to box 14 and 15 -- wait a minute. Before we go down we can see in box number 4, there's an indication of a military post, 7469, VP, military post 7469, and it says "Zvornik."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And then if you look on box 14, can you tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Box 14 says "KDK."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that you understand to mean?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And beneath that in box 15?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: For "Potpukovnik Popovic," for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go down to box 25 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You're overlapping. Both speakers should bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In box -- under box 24, can you tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That says diesel fuel, "dizel gorivo," D2.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go a little bit down the page. Okay. Can you tell us what that says?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: What I see on the screen says 140 litres were returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And if we go up and under box number 28. Do you see the amount of --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. From 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we can zoom out a little bit. Well, zoom out so we can see the whole document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, was this, to your understanding, an original document, a copy of an original document, or was this something that the OTP made up?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: No. This is a copy of an original document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to show you another document. It's P14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you really mean P14?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President? Did you say did I mean P14, 1-4? Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to avoid the confusion we had with the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, yes. I'm sorry, I don't have the record in front of me so I don't see what was recorded there. Okay. And I think we'll need to go to, as I have it here, page 148 of the B/C/S. Okay. And for the English, I think it's the same page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to read this, Ms. Frease? Maybe we can save a little time if you can just read it into the record that relates to this [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I can read most of it, but I can't -- I actually can't make out all of it. There's a -- it's the duty officer log-book from the Zvornik Brigade, and at 1400 hours there's a notation that says that Popovic was asking for -- that he should be sent a bus full of fuel and to send him 500 litres of D2, that this was requested -- that the request was made to Zlatar, the duty officer, and -- I can't read the last word, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think we have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's at page 29 of the English. In English. So maybe we can put that on the screen so everybody can see it. Okay. We have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would recommend if you continue in that way that the witness should read it in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no, no. It was absolutely fine, and I think we are all happy that you are really able to read the B/C/S text, but if you read it in B/C/S, we will receive the translation of the text immediately by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a recommendation for Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And you can see it now, I think, very clearly. In the translation it reads: "At 1400 Popovic requested a bus with a full tank and 500 litres of D2 (diesel) Zlatar Duty Officer Golic informed." Does that conform to the intercept that you were analysing in terms of verifying its accuracy, reliability and authenticity?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you another one, if I may.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this is an intercept from 16 July at 1111 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Bear with me one moment. I'll give you the P number. It's P845A.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you familiar with this intercept, Ms. Frease?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about this one.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It takes place at 1111. It's in the morning. It's a conversation between Colonel Ljubo Beara and Cerovic and a person X, and it talks about needing to conduct triage on the prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know a little bit about the context of this intercept? What I mean by that is do you know a little bit about what is meant by "triage" as has been revealed by the investigation conducted by the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I would rather not comment on the use of the word "triage."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you, did you consider the use of the word "triage" in terms of evaluating this particular intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. How so?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, because it's a word that isn't very commonly used.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you -- were you able to locate this word or locate the context of this conversation in any other material?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what material was that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It was also in the duty officer's log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: May I have P14 in e-court again, please. All right. In this case we should go to 146 in the B/C/S, and with any luck, it will be at page 27 in the English. All right. There has been some luck, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could draw your attention to the entry at 1115 hours. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: What it says is that at 1115 hours it was reported from Zlatar that triage of wounded and prisoners must be carried out, and that it was reported to Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you just remind us who is Beara in the context of this -- well, in the context of this intercept and this entry?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Colonel Beara was the chief of security for the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And just so that we're clear, this duty officer notebook belongs to what unit of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you another -- or I'd like to have you go over another example of the methods that you used in terms of authenticating this material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll need in e-court, please, P663. I understand it's 663A. Sorry. All right. We -- the translation on the left is of a different section of this intercept. Okay. It should be page -- all right. We can start here. All right. Well, we'll start here, I guess, and then we'll work our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: A conversation that took place at 1009. I know it to have taken place on the 13th of July, though it's not indicated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What I'd like to do is to move over to page 3 in the B/C/S of the document. Okay. And then we'll have to go to the next page in the English. We need ERN ending 596 in the English. There we go. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see this intercept is at 1009 as you've indicated. It involves Zoka. Can you tell us who that is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: I believe it's Zoran Malinic, who was the commander of the MPs, the military police, for the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It involves Beara, who you've already mentioned, and it involves someone named Lucic.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Who was the deputy to Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Deputy commander of the 65th Protection --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Of the MPs, right. Of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us a little bit about this conversation.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a conversation in which they're talking about the fact that so far 400 Muslims have shown up in Konjevic Polje, which is an intersection. It's the crossroads. I'm sure you know this now, but a crossroads where a lot of the column of Muslim men came through. They're talking about putting them onto a soccer field that's located just south of that intersection in Nova Kasaba and lining them up in four or five rows.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to -- I'd like to take you -- well, first of all, did you have an opportunity to examine this one and for the purposes of -- of determining its authenticity and reliability?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what else did you look at in order to determine this?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Aerial imagery. And then there were other conversations that were sort of mutually reinforcing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about the significance of the language that's used here where it reads "Hello Signor Lucic."

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a detail, but I think an important detail and the kind of details that we looked at when we analysed this material for things that stood out as being oddities, and why was it that this word "sjor" was being used here. It's a term that's used along the Dalmatian coast that means -- here it's translated as "Signor," and why would somebody like Beara be using this word. But it was consistent because Colonel Beara was posted, stationed down in Split on the Dalmatian coast for many years. So even something like this would have made the conversation and in the context internally consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have P410 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you leave this intercept, we're interested to know how do you relate this document to the soccer field you were talking about some seconds earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think on the second page it mentions Kasaba. I could be wrong. We could go to the second page. I don't see it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what is the relative location of Konjevic Polje to the soccer stadium?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's a few metres away. That -- south of that intersection of Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I was about to call up a document which I think will help clarify this somewhat, and it was P410.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could you clarify A or B?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, here's a reference in the -- in the -- sorry, I just saw it in the B/C/S version, to the "igraliste," which is soccer field. It's the playground, sort of. So it didn't specifically say Nova Kasaba playground but it says "igraliste" which means "playground." Yeah. It can be "soccer field" in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see that in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe we need to go to the next page of the English translation. Here. It says: "Put them all on the playground." About halfway through on the first page. "Shove them all on the playground ..." It's B speaking, Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: P410A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Here we have a later conversation indicated here at 2.00. Are you familiar with this intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what does this intercept relate to?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It relates -- well, it says that there are more than a thousand now and that they are at the football stadium, football field. On the football pitch would be another way to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And do you see any reference in this particular intercept to some of the same people that were referred to in the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, to Zoka.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And who would that be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P857 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Actually, let's make that P858.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you recognise what's depicted in -- what's shown in e-court now?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: It's an aerial image of the football pitch at Nova Kasaba.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. And did you consider this in determining the reliability, accuracy and authenticity of the prior two intercepts that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what did you consider in particular about this aerial image in relation to those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: The date and the time, and the fact that the analyst that provided information about this image indicated that the dark kind of rectangular shapes on the image were people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular, the date on this document is indicated as 13 July 1995 at 1400 hours?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that coincides with the intercept we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I want to show one more document. I know that we're just at the break but I think -- I'd like to show this one and hopefully it will be fast. This is -- I'd like to have P125 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: This is a document. Do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've seen it before?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And what do you recognise it to be? What is it?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Well, it's an order to the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment. It is -- the date on it is only indicated at the bottom as the 13th of July, 1995, as the -- as the date, and there's also a time of 1510 that it was delivered. At the top of the document it says that it's from Borike at 1400 hours and that it has to do with the procedure or treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did you consider this document in terms of authenticating the previous intercept that we just saw, the one at 1400 hours on 13 July?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes, because of the content also of this particular document. It starts off by saying: "There are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo (Kasaba)."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that the area in which the soccer pitch is located?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Dusanovo Kasaba is that the area that is depicted in the aerial imagery that we've just seen?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the number of prisoners that are indicated in this document, does that coincide with the number of individuals indicated in the previous intercept?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes. The second sentence of that document also says that the prisoners are under the control of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's addressed to the commander of the Military Police Battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment who you've identified as whom?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the military police battalion --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is he mentioned in the previous two intercepts that we've looked at?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: He's mentioned as Zoka. Zoka can be a nickname for Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you consider this particular document, A, relevant to the prior intercepts, and did you consider it in terms of establishing the authenticity and reliability of those intercepts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think this is a good place to stop. I appreciate your indulgence, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We have to adjourn now. This courtroom will be occupied by another Trial Chamber. We have to continue tomorrow, and you should be reminded not to communicate with either party about the content of your testimony during the break. We adjourn and resume tomorrow in the afternoon, 2.15, in this courtroom.
